exact_bound_passage.passage: SEC. 60004. STATE BORDER SECURITY REIMBURSEMENT. (a) In General.--In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security, for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $12,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to carry out this section. (b) Use of Funds.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts made available under subsection (a) to make grants to States for costs associated with actions taken on or after January 21, 2021, to assist the Federal border security missions to enforce the immigration laws, including through detention and removal, and to combat the unlawful entry of persons and contraband. (c) Application.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall develop a process for States to submit a grant application, together with satisfactory evidence of costs incurred, to seek reimbursement for any expenses described in subsection (b). (d) Prohibition.--The Secretary of Homeland Security may not make a grant for reimbursement under this section to a State if such State has received such reimbursement under any other grant program of the Department of Homeland Security.

successor_corrections.before_sentence: Section 11208(a)(1) would add fiscal year 2025 to the existing section 599D(b)(3) one-thousand allocation within the refugee admissions already allocated to the specified former-Soviet/Baltic national category described in (b)(2)(B).
successor_corrections.corrected_sentence: Section 11208(a)(1) would add fiscal year 2025 to section 599D(b)(3). Within refugee admissions already allocated under section 207(a)(3) for nationals of the independent states of the former Soviet Union, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the President must allocate one thousand admissions to the narrower section 599D(b)(2)(B) recipient category. That category consists of people who are or were nationals of those countries, are current members of the Ukrainian Catholic Church or Ukrainian Orthodox Church, and demonstrate public, active and continuous participation (or attempted participation) in the religious activities of that church. The larger nationality-based admissions allocation and this narrower religious recipient category are distinct.
successor_corrections.before_limitation: The 599D one-thousand rule operates within the specified allocated refugee admissions and its defined (b)(2)(B) category; it does not add a universal or additional overall refugee quota.
successor_corrections.corrected_limitation: The 599D(b)(3) one-thousand allocation is within the larger former-Soviet/Baltic-national refugee admissions allocation under 207(a)(3), for the narrower 599D(b)(2)(B) recipient category: are or were nationals of those countries, current Ukrainian Catholic or Ukrainian Orthodox Church members, with public, active and continuous participation (or attempted participation) in that church's religious activities. It is not an additional overall refugee quota or admission for every national or church member.

The programme's workers are not declared to be only foreign H-1B workers. Separately, 116 permanently rescinds 206000000 of unobligated funds available under INA 286(s)(2)/8 U.S.C. 1356(s)(2)bySeptember 30, 2026. That is the job-training portion of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Petitioner Account, whose dated statute assigns 50 percentof deposits to Labor; it is not all immigration fees, all Labor funding or a measured net reduction in actual services.

109 permits an employer in the seafood industry with a GRANTED H-2B petition to bring the petition's workers during 120 days beginning on its requested service start date without another petition. Crossings AFTER 90 days require two separate Sunday newspaper job orders, the appropriate Labor Electronic Job Registry and workplace posting, and offering the job to an equally or better qualified United States worker who applies and is available at the time/place of need. The corresponding exemption concerns staggering within that 120 daywindow, not every other admission, recruitment or workplace requirement. The cited INA 101(a)(15)(H)(ii)(B) temporary nonagricultural-worker definition retains foreign-residence/no-abandonment, unavailable capable U.S. workers and medical-graduate exclusions. The dated 655.5U.S. workerdefinition is broader than citizens alone and includes nationals, LPRs, refugees, asylees and other employment-authorized workers under its terms; no individual status is determined.

110 requires the H-2B prevailing-wage determination to be the GREATER of the employer's actual wage for comparable experience/qualifications in the same location OR the occupational/geographic prevailing level based on the best information at petition filing. Private wage surveys must be accepted even where OES data exist unless the Secretary finds the methodology/data statistically unsupported. exact_identity.vote-question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass
exact_identity.vote-desc: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act

substantive_actions.primary_reconstruction:
The exact choice is House suspension and passage of the complete S.3971 Senate text, the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act, on March 17, 2026. It proposes research-award security changes, an optional strategic breakthrough allocation with expressly described Phase II agreements, programme administration changes and named extensions. The sourced Immigration relationship concerns the new Phase II funding path within a programme with explicit ownership/control eligibility routes involving citizens and permanent resident aliens. The proposal does not create those status classes or turn every research, foreign-affiliation or country reference into an immigration mechanism.

Section 3 defines a strategic breakthrough allocation for an agency whose required SBIR expenditure under section 9(f)(1) exceeds $100 million: up to 0.50 percent of its extramural research budget, drawn from its SBIR allocation, for fiscal 2026 and subsequent fiscal years. This is not an additional unrestricted appropriation. The general funding-agreement permission in new (ff)(3)(B) remains distinct from the expressly described Phase II agreements in (C); the candidate does not label every possible funding permission universally Phase II. The Phase II path permits at most $30 million to a concern including its affiliates, in one award or a milestone-based series, with a project period no longer than 48 months. It requires at least one prior SBIR or STTR Phase II award, at least 100 percent matching through new private capital or new government funding outside Phase I/II arising as a result of the strategic award (or their combination), and an effective technology demonstrated by market research. DoD awards additionally require that the concern provides a product, process, or technology that meets a necessary level of readiness and has a commitment for inclusion in a programme objective memorandum from an official with the rank of programme acquisition executive or higher in a DoD acquisition organisation; provides a product, process, or technology that will meet high priority requirements or operational needs of a military department through a successful transition and into the acquisition process; and demonstrates that at least 20 percent of the required matching funds come from new DoD funding under a programme other than Phase I or II of SBIR or STTR as a result of an award using the strategic breakthrough allocation. Eligible activities must be critical technology areas or requirements the agency deems necessary. The agency must consider the printed alternative selection criteria for national-security capability, new technologies/processes/applications, expressed customer purchase/integration intent, or undercapitalized technology; streamline proposals, and complete any contract awards it makes within 90 days of receiving the relevant proposal; this is not guaranteed approval. The named (aa)(1)/(4) amount/agency-waiver requirements are waived for qualifying strategic awards up to $30 million, not every programme eligibility rule. Eligible agencies brief Congress within 60 days about plans to use or not use the authority, with recurring briefings for agencies opting in until procedures are finalized.

The dated section 121.702 rule expressly applies eligibility at award of SBIR/STTR Phase I or II funding agreements. Its SBIR individual/qualified-business branch requires more than 50 percent direct ownership AND control through citizens or permanent resident aliens, or the separately named qualified businesses, Indian tribe/ANC/NHO or wholly owned institutional businesses, and permitted combinations. Distinct SBIR majority ownership by multiple venture-capital operating companies, hedge funds/private-equity firms requires the relevant agency election under 15 U.S.C. 638(dd); qualified joint ventures and the single-fund restriction remain separate. The STTR branch does not acquire SBIR's multiple-venture-fund alternative. ESOP/trust treatment, size/affiliation and joint-venture exceptions, and ownership calculations remain programme-specific. The dated statutory (dd) route also retains agency ceilings of 25 percent for NIH/Energy/NSF and 15 percent for other participating agencies, written determination/notice, registration and the qualified nine-month delayed-award/changed-ownership exception with all other award requirements. These are not citizen-only companies, all-owner or all-worker citizenship requirements, and they do not determine any person's admission or employment authorization.

The published January 16, 2025 amendment to 121.702(c)(7) is read separately from the January 1 edition. It excludes a concern with an other-than-small ostensible subcontractor from small-business treatment for these awards, preserves the primary/vital-work or unusual-reliance predicates and performance review, and expressly requires the prime and any small-business ostensible subcontractor to meet applicable (a)/(b) ownership/control requirements individually. This known material amendment is applied; no exhaustive later policy or individual company eligibility is certified. The attempted 2026 annual-edition response was HTML, not governing law, and is not used as a rule or evidence of universal source unavailability. The new expressly described Phase II path can engage existing status-conditioned programme eligibility without inventing a new personal status class; its other qualification routes remain intact. This is a source-grounded candidate application for review, not a final legal judgment for a company or worker.

Section 2 changes company-award security duties. It removes the old (g)(15)/(o)(19) conjunction requiring both a listed foreign relationship and an additional interference/duplication/conflict/disclosure/law/national-security harm. The three retained malign-talent/location/research-affiliation branches and new list-linked, classified-source and agency-determined-risk alternatives remain under the agency-head determination. SBIR's security-risk wording and STTR's printed foreign-risk wording are not homogenized. New evaluation/due-diligence provisions cover cybersecurity, patents, employees, foreign ownership and financial obligations, affiliations, investments, licensing/joint ventures, business relationships and specified lists using a risk-based approach as appropriate. Covered individual requires substantive meaningful research contribution AND agency designation; foreign affiliations, countries of concern and the incorporated malign-talent definition are not generic personal nationality labels. Agency notification is as appropriate pursuant to its discretion without compromising security, and a denial does not prohibit eligibility in a subsequent cycle. Repayment and ongoing-disclosure provisions retain their qualified agency national-security determinations and renumbered references. These are company-award mechanisms, not a universal visa/admission, immigration-status or individual misconduct determination.

The new proposal limits apply equally to concerns for fiscal 2027 and later, using the director's selected fiscal-year/solicitation/topic method and the exact scope of Phase I solicitations and Phase II solicitations under subsection (cc), across all agency components. The director sets the limit at least 90 days before the start of the fiscal year. Topic waivers require an urgent time-sensitive mission need, written justification, undersecretary/Administrator approval or disapproval within 15 days of the undersecretary receiving the request and written justification, nondelegation, the five-percent topic ceiling and retained notice/records; these are not waivers of all ownership/size conditions. Phase III training, procurement advocacy, standardized procedures/data/contract references and commercialization support remain distinct from Phase I/II eligibility. Section 3(b) expands the identified readiness-programme research pool to strategic-allocation awardees, adds budget-process analysis and congressional integration information, and deletes the old (y)(3) written military-secretary certification that successful Phase III transition is expected to meet high-priority military requirements. That deletion does not remove the separate new strategic-allocation DoD predicates. Retained readiness-programme administrative funding remains limited to one percent and cannot fund Phase III awards; new direct access to potential Phase III purchasers does not guarantee a purchase. Technical/business assistance allows up to $6,500 per Phase I project and $50,000 per Phase II project, as part of or in addition to the award as the agency determines, with vendor or staff/training uses and I-Corps options; foreign-involvement screening does not alone classify workers by immigration status.

The subsection (cc) direct-to-Phase-II authority retains the agency-head determination that the concern completed the substantive Phase I determinations even without a Phase I award. Section 10(a) extends that authority to September 30, 2031, adds Energy and NASA to NIH, Defense and Education, and adds STTR alongside SBIR. This affects a Phase II award path subject to the programme-specific ownership/control routes, not merely an agency name. Programme and named pilot sunsets change from the printed 2025 endpoints to 2031; this does not certify uninterrupted operation or current agency policy. Remaining fiscal-2026 required funds may carry into fiscal 2027 under the named conditions. Strategic section 3 and its amendments cease on September 30, 2031 with restoration as if not enacted. The SOCOM pilot uses the published 2024 note expressly amended by 2021 Public Law 117-81 section 852: covered-entity transfers are bounded to ten percent per fiscal year and $20 million aggregate; intermediary costs are excluded; covered awards are SBIR awards. New termination changes its (e) September 2025 endpoint to 2031, while its separate annual-report endpoint remains October 1, 2026. Original 2019 (d)/2021 wording is historical, not silently substituted for the amended target. The bill extends the 2022 foreign-risk study's annual reporting period from three to eight years without changing its initial one-year deadline, and separately repeals the triennial venture-capital/hedge/private-equity impact study codified at 15 U.S.C. 638a; it does not abolish all GAO reporting or establish study results.

Yea and Nay concern this entire exact suspension-passage package, not a separate vote on owner statuses, security rules or any grant component. No motive, preferred alternative, actual award, research result, company/individual qualification, immigration outcome, current consolidated-law certificate, editorial acceptance or publication is inferred.
